Battery storage system result metrics across 2030 price scenarios 50 3.6 Optimized Individual EV Charging Results As described in Section 2.3.4, we conducted a supplemental EV charging simulation analysis to determine the optimal charging behavior for various price signals under different scenarios of driving behavior. Figure 34 shows a sample result for a single driver’s optimal charging behavior when responding to the SCE 2030 residential “Full” dynamic price during two weeks of the year. The left side shows a week of summer prices that encourages the driver to do fewer, longer charging sessions, which differs from behavior under the winter profile that encourages short charging sessions every day. Note that the optimization was run in 1-week increments, with the battery state of charge (SOC) starting and ending at 0.75 for each week. Additionally, there is no benefit in the model to keeping the battery at a high state of charge “just in case”, therefore just-in-time charging is generally preferred to minimize passive losses. Future work can explore adjusting the model to consider customer’s preference for keeping their battery at a relatively high SOC. Figure 34. EV charging optimization inputs and results for two weeks across the year, Looking across all customers modeled, and across the entire year, we can start to explore how optimal charging profiles vary by price profile and driving patterns. Figure 35 shows the optimized charging demand for the average day of the year, for five clusters of customers that span the range of daily driving demands. The two panels show the response to two price profiles; as shown, drivers charge more in the early morning hours on the Mild tariff than on the Full, when load is more concentrated in the daytime. The lines in Figure 35 show the drastic variation in charging across clusters of drivers. Cluster 0 has the lowest driving energy demands, and only meaningfully charges between 8am and 2pm, when prices tend to be lowest in each week (though not necessarily each day). Cluster 9 has the highest driving energy 51 demand and shows significant amounts of early morning charging as well as some late night charging sessions, in addition to the daytime demands. Figure 35. Average daily optimized EV charging profile for customers in five clusters of daily driving behavior, in response to two price profiles While the above figure shows the diversity of charging patterns, it does not appropriately represent the most common drivers. The underlying driving data comes from a population-wide simulation of the San Francisco Bay Area, and clusters of drivers were sampled proportionally to how common a given cluster was in the area.
